issues.legal_issue: A statutory clearance procedure that gives affected tenants opportunities to object and appeal imposes reasonable restrictions on their property interests.
material_facts: The tenants had interests in the premises that were affected by the clearance order.
The statutory scheme provided for public notice and an opportunity for affected persons to object to the proposed order.
The scheme also provided affected persons a right of appeal against the confirmed order.
issues.conclusion: The restrictions on the tenants’ property interests were reasonable, so the statutory provisions were valid.
issues.legal_principle: A tenant’s interest in demised premises is property protected by Article 19(1)(f), but Article 19(5) permits reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public. The provisions must be read together: public notice permits affected tenants to object, the authority has duties concerning persons likely to be displaced, and an affected person may appeal. Those safeguards make the restrictions reasonable.

rule.if: clearance_order_proceeding and tenant_property_interest_affected and tenants_have_objection_opportunity and tenants_have_appeal_opportunity

predicates.clearance_order_proceeding: A public authority undertook a proceeding to clear an area and remove buildings in it.
predicates.tenant_property_interest_affected: Tenants held interests in premises that would be affected by the clearance order.
predicates.tenants_have_objection_opportunity: The procedure gave affected tenants an opportunity to object to the proposed clearance order.
predicates.tenants_have_appeal_opportunity: The procedure gave affected persons an opportunity to appeal the confirmed clearance order.

issues.definition: When a clearance proceeding affects tenants’ property interests and gives them opportunities to object and appeal, the restrictions imposed on those interests are reasonable and valid.

issues.legal_issue: Tenants affected by a confirmed clearance order are persons aggrieved who must use the appeal remedy, and cannot pursue a suit if they do not appeal or their appeal is dismissed.
material_facts: The plaintiffs were tenants whose occupation would be affected by the confirmed clearance order.
They brought a suit challenging the order and did not pursue the available appeal.
The order became final subject to the outcome of an appeal by an aggrieved person.
issues.conclusion: The tenants were persons aggrieved entitled to appeal, and their suit was not maintainable because the statutory appeal was the available remedy.
issues.legal_principle: The expression “person aggrieved” includes a person whose legal interest is affected by an order; the Court relied on Ex parte Sidebotham, In re Sidebotham and Sharifuddin v. R. P. Singh. Under the appeal and finality scheme in Schedule GG, an affected tenant may appeal the confirmed order, but a suit is not available if no appeal is filed or an appeal is dismissed.

predicates.tenant_challenges_confirmed_clearance_or: A tenant brought a proceeding challenging a confirmed order to clear an area.
predicates.tenant_is_affected_by_order: The order affected the tenant’s legal interest or occupation of premises.
predicates.appeal_not_filed: The affected tenant did not file the available appeal against the order.
predicates.tenant_appeal_dismissed: The affected tenant filed an appeal, and that appeal was dismissed.

issues.definition: An affected tenant who challenges a confirmed clearance order cannot maintain a suit if the tenant did not appeal or the tenant’s appeal was dismissed.

issues.legal_issue: An amendment to pleadings should not be allowed when it introduces a new fraud case with no factual basis in the original pleading.
material_facts: The original plaint characterized the action as mala fide on grounds concerning the validity of the statutory provisions and the absence of an opportunity to be heard.
The amendment alleged that the landlords had fraudulently and wrongfully induced the authority to make the clearance order.
The original plaint contained no factual basis for that fraud allegation.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in allowing the amendment because it introduced a new case of fraud that had no basis in the original plaint.
issues.legal_principle: A party should not be permitted to make out a new case by amending a pleading. The bare use of the term “mala fide” does not justify an amendment that changes the case into one of fraud when the original pleading contains no factual foundation for that allegation.

predicates.civil_appeal_reviewing_pleading_amendmen: An appellate court was reviewing an order permitting an amendment to a pleading.
predicates.amendment_introduces_new_fraud_case: The proposed amendment alleged fraud that was not part of the original case.
predicates.original_pleading_lacks_factual_basis: The original pleading did not state facts supporting the later fraud allegation.

issues.definition: An amendment introducing a fraud case unsupported by the original pleading’s facts should not be allowed.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may admit additional evidence only when a permitted ground exists, including when the evidence is necessary to enable it to pronounce judgment, and may not use that power to order a virtual retrial when the existing record permits decision.
material_facts: The High Court relied on documents already in the record that it considered supportive of the tenants’ allegations if unexplained.
The High Court did not identify a lacuna in the evidence or state that it needed additional evidence to pronounce judgment.
The High Court remitted the matter for additional evidence and a virtual retrial.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not entitled to admit additional evidence or remit the case for a virtual retrial in those circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits additional evidence only on the grounds specified in the rule, including where the appellate court needs it to pronounce judgment. It does not permit evidence to be added merely to reach a particular result; its use is limited to a proper need such as removing a lacuna. A general retrial cannot be ordered under that rule, and the requirements for remand under Order XLI, rules 23 and 25 were not met.

rule.if: civil_appeal_reviewing_evidence and existing_record_permits_judgment and additional_evidence_not_needed_to_enable_judgment and appellate_court_orders_virtual_retrial

predicates.civil_appeal_reviewing_evidence: An appellate court was considering whether to receive further evidence in a civil appeal.
predicates.existing_record_permits_judgment: The evidence already on the record could be considered and a judgment could be pronounced on that record.
predicates.additional_evidence_not_needed_to_enable: The appellate court did not need further evidence in order to pronounce judgment.
predicates.appellate_court_orders_virtual_retrial: The appellate court directed a new evidentiary hearing that amounted in substance to a retrial.

issues.definition: When the existing record permits judgment and further evidence is not needed to pronounce it, an appellate court may not admit that evidence and order a virtual retrial.

issues.legal_issue: A court may not virtually oblige a party to examine a particular witness.
material_facts: The High Court stated that it particularly wanted specified public officials and the defendants to be examined on the disputed issue.
The direction could cause the parties to treat examination of those witnesses as effectively compulsory.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its competence by directing the parties to examine particular witnesses.
issues.legal_principle: A court cannot compel a party to make a particular pleading or amendment, and likewise cannot virtually oblige a party to examine a particular witness.

predicates.civil_appellate_proceeding: A court was hearing a civil matter at the appellate stage.
predicates.court_directs_party_to_examine_specific_: The court directed a party to examine a witness selected by the court.

issues.definition: In an appellate civil proceeding, a court that directs a party to examine a particular witness may not virtually compel that examination.
